headline: A thousand unique transforms splits the field three ways: the CSS-variable lanes hold constant work, `cn` and the runtimes pay per value, and `@yak/solid` pays for a reactive wrapper it will never use.

microbench.why: `vanilla-solid` leads at 2.18M renders/s writing an inline style directly. `next-yak-css` at 1.58M and `bamboo` at 1.57M turn the value into a CSS variable and keep per-instance work constant, while `styled-components` at 211,000 emits a rule per value and `goober` at 169,000 hashes one. This is the case that separates the two Tailwind mergers: `cnfast` holds 557,000 and `cn` falls to 243,000, below `tailwind-merge` at 477,000, because a unique arbitrary-value utility per element misses every cache. `yak-solid` at 110,000 is last, and its own runtime accounts for only 0.945 ms of the 11.3 ms: a dynamic interpolation takes the non-folded path, so every element gets a Solid component with a memo over its props — machinery that exists to make updates cheap, running in a server render that will never update.

autocannon.why: `next-yak-css` at 1,280 req/s and `vanilla` at 1,190 lead. `cn` at 235 req/s serves less than half of `cnfast`'s 489, and `yak-solid` at 100 is last, its per-element memo constructed inside every request.

attribution.why: `bamboo` at 0.778 ms, `next-yak-css` at 0.785 ms and `vanilla-solid` at 0.810 ms lead with empty lib buckets. `cn` spends 4.20 of its 4.59 ms inside its own package — 92% of the render — against 1.86 of 2.60 ms for `cnfast` and 1.82 of 2.40 ms for `tailwind-merge`, so the miss path costs `cn` more than twice what either of the others pays. `styled-components` needs 5.25 ms with 4.73 ms of lib: a thousand unique values means a thousand rules. `yak-solid`'s 11.3 ms is 88% framework, the reactive scope per element rather than the variable itself.

hydrate.why: `vanilla-solid` at 31.1 ms leads and the React lanes cluster near 50 ms. `yak-solid` at 94.0 ms rebuilds the same per-element memos while attaching. `goober` at 1,300 ms is the suite's worst reading, inserting one rule per unique value into the document during hydration.

top3.label: StyleX without CSS layers (:not() specificity hack)

inp.why: `stylex-layers` at 6.5 ms leads and most React lanes answer near 7.5 ms. `cn` at 17.0 ms pays its cache miss again on the update, more than twice `cnfast`'s 7.9 ms. `goober` at 23.2 ms and `panda-props` at 28.9 ms re-hash or re-resolve every value, which is what a per-value class costs when the value actually moves.

mount.why: `next-yak-css` mounts in 61.6 ms and `vanilla-solid` in 22.2 ms. `goober` at 1,290 ms and `panda-props` at 103 ms pay their per-value insertion before the first paint. `yak-solid` at 75.1 ms sits with the React field, since its per-element cost is JavaScript that overlaps the browser's layout work.

renderTiming.why: One style recalculation per lane. A CSS variable on an inline style never invalidates the sheet, so the lanes that avoid a class per value all reach the style engine with the same single match.

payload.why: `vanilla` at 5,502 gz B and the next-yak css-prop lanes near 5,580 B are the floor. The per-value lanes lose here as they lose everywhere: `emotion` ships 18,347 B of CSS and `styled-components` 13,838 B for a thousand rules. `cn` at 23,438 B carries 13,054 B of library JS, the most of any lane in the case, and `yak-solid` at 12,016 B keeps its CSS to 97 B and pays in hydration-keyed markup instead.

nsweep.why: `vanilla-solid` holds 1.74 ms at 4,000 instances and `bamboo` 2.74 ms. `goober` at 156 ms, `yak-solid` at 37.3 ms and `cn` at 18.9 ms have the steepest lines, for three different reasons: a rule per value, a reactive scope per element, and a cache miss per element.

crossCase: The naive corner of the dynamic trio with the Examples `dyn-fair` and `dyn-inline`. On React the three read 801,000, 792,000 and 1.56M renders/s for `next-yak`: the CSS-variable path costs it about half the inline-style control, and that control is what a developer reaches by hand-splitting static class from dynamic style. On Solid the same three read 110,000, 113,000 and 2.16M for `yak-solid` — the inline-style control is at parity with hand-written Solid while the variable path is twenty times behind it. `cn` shows the third pattern: 243,000 here against 1.60M on the best-practice case, so its whole loss is the cache miss.
